items.context: The topology lens adds clustering logic, edge styling, node capping, and 15+ inspector actions. The workspace shell used a store-first testing approach (unit test stores extensively, component tests verify wiring not React Flow internals). The question is whether to follow the same pattern or adapt it for topology-specific concerns like clustering state transitions and edge aggregation.

options.label: Store-first + clustering utility tests
options.rationale: Follow the shell's store-first pattern. Unit test clustering transformations (API nodes → parent-child hierarchy, collapse/expand state, edge aggregation, node capping) as pure utility functions in a dedicated `clustering-utils.ts` with co-located tests. Test action registry factories return correct action objects. Component tests verify cluster nodes render rollup counts and that expand/collapse dispatches correct store actions. Skip testing React Flow's parent-child rendering internals. Recommended because clustering logic is the highest-complexity area and is testable as pure functions, while React Flow's sub-flow rendering is framework behavior we shouldn't re-test.

options.label: Visual snapshot testing for clusters
options.rationale: Add Playwright or Storybook snapshot tests that capture the visual appearance of collapsed/expanded clusters, edge styles, and the MiniMap. Higher confidence in visual correctness but slower, more brittle, and harder to maintain. Would require setting up visual testing infrastructure that doesn't exist yet.

items.topic: Dagre layout + React Flow parent-child integration approach
items.context: Round 1 decided on React Flow sub-flows (parent-child nodes) for clustering. However, Dagre layout doesn't natively understand React Flow's parent-child containment — Dagre positions all nodes in a flat graph. This means child nodes may be positioned outside their parent's bounds. The layout integration needs a specific strategy to ensure children are positioned correctly inside parent cluster boundaries.

options.label: Two-pass layout: Dagre for inter-cluster, then relative positioning for intra-cluster
options.rationale: First pass: run Dagre with only cluster nodes (initiatives + unassigned + unclustered items) to get cluster-level layout. Second pass: for each expanded cluster, run a sub-Dagre layout on its children to position them relative to the parent's origin. Parent node dimensions are computed from children's bounding box + padding. Recommended because it cleanly separates inter-cluster and intra-cluster layout, works well with React Flow's parent-child coordinate system (children use coordinates relative to parent), and scales predictably.

options.label: Dagre compound graph (cluster support)
options.rationale: Use Dagre's built-in cluster/subgraph support (`setParent()` on nodes) to compute all positions in one pass. Dagre allocates space for clusters and positions children inside. Simpler single-pass approach but Dagre's cluster support is known to have edge cases with edge routing and the cluster sizing can be unpredictable.

items.topic: Inspector action endpoint audit — handling missing endpoints
items.context: The 15+ topology inspector actions need to call existing API endpoints. After auditing the swarm-manager API, most actions map to existing endpoints (backlog CRUD, captures classify, initiatives update). However, some actions may need lightweight composition: 'Create item from suggestion' (capture → backlog item) and 'Assign initiative' (update backlog item's initiative field) may not have dedicated endpoints but can be composed from existing primitives. The question is how to handle actions that don't map 1:1 to an existing endpoint.

options.label: Compose from existing endpoints client-side
options.rationale: For actions like 'Create item from suggestion', call the existing backlog create endpoint with pre-filled fields from the capture data. For 'Assign initiative', call the existing backlog update endpoint with the initiative field. No new API endpoints needed. Recommended because it keeps the API surface small, avoids scope creep, and these compositions are simple (1-2 sequential API calls).

options.label: Add thin API convenience endpoints
options.rationale: Create purpose-built endpoints like `POST /api/v1/captures/:id/create-item` and `PATCH /api/v1/backlog/:kind/:name/assign-initiative`. Cleaner client code, atomic operations, but adds API surface and is technically out of scope (plan says no new endpoints unless insufficient).

items.context: The edge differentiation strategy (R1 d2) uses color + dash pattern for 4 edge types. Users need a way to learn the mapping. The plan mentions 'a legend in the canvas corner' but the specific placement and behavior needs to be decided.

options.label: Compact fixed legend in bottom-left corner
options.rationale: A small floating panel (similar to MiniMap in bottom-right) showing 4 rows: colored line sample + edge type name. Always visible when topology lens is active. Collapsible via a toggle. Recommended because it's always discoverable without interaction, doesn't overlap with MiniMap (opposite corner), and follows common graph visualization conventions.

options.label: Legend in sidebar footer
options.rationale: Place the edge legend at the bottom of the sidebar. Only visible when sidebar is open. Saves canvas space but hidden when sidebar is collapsed, reducing discoverability.

options.label: No persistent legend — tooltip on edge hover only
options.rationale: Edge type shown only on hover. Cleanest canvas but requires interaction to learn the system. Users may not realize edges have different meanings.

items.text: Skill discovery found no React Flow-specific skills in the prompt-manager library. The existing skills (react-coherence, ux, test) are already in Required Reading and cover general patterns. No additional skills needed for this item — the implementation details are React Flow API-specific and best informed by the workspace shell's established patterns.
